analogy.p: Imagine a chef invents a unique dish and writes the recipe. Anyone can buy a meal, but copying the recipe card, selling the chef's dish under your own name or giving it out for free would take away the chef's income and credit. Copyright law is the rule that the chef decides who may copy the recipe. A software licence is like the restaurant's terms of entry: you may eat here, but you may not photocopy the secret recipe. The analogy breaks down because recipes can be cooked from ideas anyone may reuse, whereas software copying is exact and costs nothing, so copies are perfect and spread globally in seconds.

bullets: It is a **UK law** passed in 1988; it protects intellectual property (creations of the mind) rather than physical property.
It protects the **creator's rights**: the right to decide who can copy, distribute, adapt and perform their work.
It protects the **creator's income**: if copies are free and illegal, fewer people buy the genuine product.
It applies to **software** because computer programs are legally treated as a type of written (literary) work.
It is a **criminal and civil** matter: owners can sue for damages and serious cases can lead to prosecution.
Exam link: it sits in the same spec section (1.6) as the **Data Protection Act 2018** and **Computer Misuse Act 1990**; do not mix them up.
core.h: What the Act is and why it exists
core.p: The **Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988** (often shortened to **CDPA 1988**) is a UK law that gives the creator of an original piece of work legal control over how that work is used. Creating software, a song, a film or a photograph takes time, skill and money, so the law stops other people simply copying the finished product and profiting from it without the creator's permission. Without this protection there would be little financial reason to develop new software or content. In OCR J277 it is one of the three pieces of legislation you must know for Computer Science, alongside the **Data Protection Act 2018** and the **Computer Misuse Act 1990**.

bullets: **Software**: the source code and the compiled program are both protected as the creator's work.
**Music and films**: sound recordings, film footage and broadcasts are protected.
**Text and images**: articles, books, photographs, diagrams and artwork are protected.
**Video games**: protected as software, and their artwork, music and characters are protected too.
Protection is **automatic**; a copyright symbol (c) is helpful as a reminder but is not required by law.
Duration: copyright generally lasts for the creator's **lifetime plus 70 years** for most written, musical and artistic works.
Copyright belongs to the **creator or their employer** (a programmer working for a company usually creates software that the company owns).
core.h: What is protected: types of work
core.p: Copyright covers a wide range of original creative and technical work. The key idea for the exam is that it is not just books and music: **computer programs, databases, websites, images, video games, films, recorded music and written text** are all protected. Protection exists as soon as the work is created and fixed in some form (for example saved as a file), so the creator does not need to pay to register it. Ideas on their own are not protected, only the particular way they are expressed.

bullets: Making **copies of software, music or films** and giving or selling them to others without permission.
**Downloading or uploading** pirated copies, for example through torrent or file-sharing sites.
**Installing one licensed copy on many computers** when the licence covers only one (or a set number).
**Using software without a licence**, or after a trial licence has expired, by bypassing the check.
**Cracking or removing** licence-key checks or copy protection so the software runs without paying.
**Modifying and redistributing** someone else's program as if it were your own, or claiming their work as yours.
**Selling** copies of another person's work for profit without permission.
core.p: The central rule is that you must not copy, share or use protected work without the permission of the copyright holder. In computing, this mostly means **software piracy**: making illegal copies of software, or using software that was copied illegally. Permission is normally given through a **software licence**, which is a legal agreement stating how many people can install and use the program and what they may do with it. Anything beyond the terms of the licence is a breach.

bullets: Large-scale piracy: **counterfeit copies** or websites sharing **cracked** software.
Small-scale piracy: **casual copying** between friends or installing one copy on many machines.
Consequences for the **owner**: lost sales, lost revenue, less money for development and support.
Consequences for the **user**: pirated copies often contain **malware**, receive **no updates or support**, and may stop working.
Consequences for the **offender**: possible **fines, legal action and criminal prosecution**.
Organisations can also break the Act by accident (**under-licensing**), for example buying 10 licences but installing on 30 computers.
Sharing your **licence key** online with others counts as breaking the terms of the licence.
core.p: **Software piracy** means the illegal copying, distribution or use of software. It can be large-scale (a gang producing counterfeit discs or running a website hosting cracked programs) or small-scale (a friend giving you a copy of a game they bought). Both are illegal because the copyright holder has not agreed and has not been paid. Piracy hurts developers by reducing sales, which can lead to higher prices for genuine customers, less money to fix bugs and make new products, and job losses in the industry.

bullets: **Single-user licence**: one installation or one user only.
**Multi-user / network licence**: a set number of users can use the software at once.
**Site licence**: an organisation such as a school can install on all its machines, usually for a bigger fee.
**Trial / shareware**: free use for a limited period or with limited features, after which you must buy a licence.
The **End User Licence Agreement (EULA)** is the text you agree to when installing; it lists what you may and may not do.
Link to the other spec point: **open source** licences give extra freedoms (see the Open source and proprietary software note), but they are still licences and still protected by copyright law.
core.h: Software licences and how they link to the Act
core.p: When you buy software you do not usually buy the program itself, you buy a **licence** that gives you permission to use it under stated conditions. This is what makes the Act practical: the licence tells you exactly what is legal. A **single-user licence** allows one person on one device, a **multi-user** or **site licence** allows a stated number of users or a whole organisation, and a **free trial** allows use for a limited time. If you break these conditions you are infringing copyright even though you bought a legitimate copy.

bullets: **Licence key / product key**: a unique code typed in during installation; the software refuses to run if the code is invalid or already used too many times.
**Online activation**: the software contacts the publisher's server to check the key and may limit how many devices can activate.
**Digital Rights Management (DRM)**: software that controls how digital content is used, for example stopping copying or limiting devices.
**Dongle or hardware key**: a physical device that must be plugged in for expensive software to run.
**Watermarking** and visible ownership notices: hidden or visible marks showing who owns the work and helping to trace leaked copies.
**Legal action**: the publisher can take pirates to court and the Act supports fines and prosecution.
**Education and licensing terms**: the EULA and awareness campaigns tell users that copying is illegal.
Cloud/subscription models make piracy harder because the software runs on a server or must regularly check in.
core.h: How software owners prevent illegal copying
core.p: Because copying digital files is cheap and easy, owners combine technical protection with legal protection. Technical methods make it hard to use a copy without paying; legal methods make it risky to try. No method is perfect because determined pirates can sometimes break protection, which is why both approaches are used together. In exam answers, always say how the method works, not just its name.

bullets: Burning copies of a bought video game and **selling them** at school: breaks the Act.
A company buys **5 licences** but installs the program on **25 computers**: breaks the Act (and the licence).
Downloading a **cracked** version of paid software from a file-sharing site: breaks the Act.
Sharing your **account login for a streaming service** with a stranger: breaches the licence terms; the point to stress is that you are using it beyond the permission given.
Copying a **paragraph or photograph** from a website into your own project and pretending it is yours: breaches copyright.
Hacking into someone's account to read their emails: that is the **Computer Misuse Act**, not copyright.
Using personal data in a way the person did not agree to: **Data Protection Act**.
core.h: Applying the Act to scenarios (exam skill)
core.p: Questions usually describe a situation and ask which law is broken. Use a simple routine: identify what was done with someone else's creation, ask whether permission or a licence allowed it, and name the Act with a reason. If the scenario is about copying, sharing, selling or using someone's creative work or software without permission, it is the **Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988**. If it is about gaining access to a computer or files without permission, it is the **Computer Misuse Act 1990**. If it is about how personal data is stored and used, it is the **Data Protection Act 2018**.

bullets: **Civil action**: the owner sues for damages and an order to stop (an injunction).
**Criminal prosecution**: possible for serious, commercial-scale copying and selling.
**Fines** and, in serious cases, **imprisonment**.
**Reputation and business damage**: a firm caught using unlicensed software can be audited and fined.
Software industry bodies carry out **licence audits** of companies to check they have enough licences.
Remember: **ignorance is not a defence**; owners must still be paid even if you did not realise copying was illegal.
core.h: Penalties and who can enforce the Act
core.p: The copyright owner (or a body acting for them) can take **civil action**, asking a court to order the offender to stop, to hand over illegal copies and to pay damages for the money lost. Where infringement is deliberate and on a commercial scale, it can also be treated as a **criminal offence**, leading to fines and possibly prison. You do not need to remember exact sentences for J277; you need to know that there are real legal consequences.

bullets: A **backup copy** is allowed if the licence says so.
**Quoting a short extract** with credit for review or study can be fair dealing.
Copying an **entire** paid program to avoid buying it is not allowed.
**Creative Commons** and open source licences give permission in advance, so using the work as the licence states is legal.
Always **check the licence** or terms before using someone else's content.
Giving **credit** (acknowledging the source) does not by itself make copying legal if permission is needed.
core.p: The Act does not stop all copying. UK law allows limited **fair dealing** for purposes such as private study, research, criticism or review, and quotation with proper credit. Software licences often allow you to make one **backup copy** for security. The important point is that copying which stays within the law or within the terms of the licence is acceptable; copying that replaces buying the product is not. For J277 you mostly need the principle that permission is what makes copying legal.

bullets: For protection: creators and small developers rely on **sales** to continue working.
For protection: legal software is **safer** and supported.
Against strict controls: some users cannot afford genuine software.
Against strict controls: **DRM** can inconvenience honest customers (for example limiting devices).
Open source shows an alternative model where creators **choose** to share freely.
Stakeholders often named in answers: **software companies, employees, customers, governments**.
core.p: Alongside the law you may be asked about the **ethical** side. Supporters of strong copyright argue that creators deserve payment and that piracy is theft of effort. Critics note that high prices, region restrictions and lack of access push some people to pirate, and that very long copyright periods can limit sharing of knowledge. A balanced answer gives both views and links to **stakeholders**: developers, publishers, consumers, schools and businesses.

bullets: **Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988**: protects creators' work; offences are copying, sharing or using without permission.
**Computer Misuse Act 1990**: offences are unauthorised access, access with intent to commit further crimes, and unauthorised modification or impairment of data/computers (such as viruses and DoS).
**Data Protection Act 2018**: the UK's implementation of GDPR; controls how organisations collect, store and use personal data, and gives individuals rights over it.
A hacker who steals a game's source code could break **both** Computer Misuse (access) and Copyright (copying/distributing).
Keywords: **copy / share / pirate / licence = Copyright**; **hack / access / virus = Computer Misuse**; **personal data / consent = Data Protection**.
core.h: Comparing the three laws you must know
core.p: J277 groups three Acts together and a very common mistake is to attach the wrong one to a scenario. A good way to separate them is by asking what is being **harmed**: creators' work (Copyright), the security of computer systems (Computer Misuse) or individuals' personal data (Data Protection).

bullets: Link to **malware**: cracked software often hides trojans, spyware or ransomware.
Link to **networks**: peer-to-peer file sharing is a common way illegal copies spread.
Link to **open source vs proprietary**: licence type decides what copying and modifying is legal.
Link to **cloud storage and streaming**: terms of service limit sharing of paid accounts and content.
Link to **stakeholders**: owners, users, employees and governments are affected differently.
Link to **testing and development**: businesses must keep records of licences as part of good IT management.
core.p: This point connects to several other parts of the course. It links to **software types** (licensing of operating systems and utility software), **networks and security** (piracy often happens over the internet using file sharing), **malware** (pirated software is a common route for infection) and to **ethical, legal, cultural and environmental impacts** more widely. In long-answer questions, linking these ideas is how you reach the top mark band.

exam: Identify the Act first: copying, sharing, selling or using software/music/films without permission = **Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988**.
1-mark questions: state the name of the law or the offence (for example 'software piracy' or 'copying software without permission').
2-mark 'describe' questions: give the action and the reason it is illegal, such as 'installing one licensed copy on many computers breaks the licence and copyright law'.
Prevention methods: name the method AND say how it works (for example 'a licence key must be entered, so the software will not run without a valid code').
3-mark answers on consequences: use owner (lost sales), user (malware, no support) and offender (fines or prosecution).
For 'which law' scenario tables, underline keywords in the scenario before choosing: copy/share/licence, access/hack, personal data.
For 6-mark discuss questions, give both sides (benefits to creators vs drawbacks for users such as cost and DRM) and finish with a justified conclusion.
Use precise vocabulary: **licence, piracy, copyright holder, permission, infringe**; avoid vague words like 'stealing' without explaining.
Do not name more than the question asks for; extra incorrect laws can cancel marks in 'identify the law' questions.
Link answers to the scenario given (name the software, the company or the user) rather than writing generic statements.

mistakes.r: Hacking is the Computer Misuse Act 1990. The Copyright, Designs and Patents Act is about copying, sharing and using protected work without permission.
mistakes.w: Copyright law is about stopping hackers.

mistakes.r: Acknowledging the author does not replace permission; copying protected work without permission still infringes copyright unless the law or licence allows it.
mistakes.w: If I give credit to the author, copying is always legal.

mistakes.r: Copying and sharing without permission is illegal even if you make no money, for example giving pirated software to a friend.
mistakes.w: It is only illegal if I sell the copies.

mistakes.r: You buy a licence with conditions; installing on more devices than the licence allows breaks the licence and the Act.
mistakes.w: Buying software means I own it and can do what I like.

mistakes.r: UK copyright applies automatically when the work is created; the (c) symbol is not required.
mistakes.w: Copyright must be registered with a symbol.

mistakes.r: They make copying harder but can be cracked or shared, so owners also use activation, DRM and legal action.
It also harms small developers, employees and honest users, and pirated software can contain malware and has no support.
The Data Protection Act 2018 protects personal data; software is protected by copyright law.
mistakes.w: The Data Protection Act protects software.

summary: You must know that the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988 protects the work of creators (including software, music, films, text and images) by making it illegal to copy, share, modify or sell their work without permission, and be able to apply it to scenarios such as software piracy. It matters because Paper 1 ethical/legal questions ask you to identify which law is broken, explain why, and describe how software owners prevent illegal copying.

terms.d: The legal right of the creator of an original work to control how it is copied, distributed and adapted.
UK law that protects the intellectual property of creators, including software, by making unauthorised copying and distribution illegal.
The illegal copying, distribution or use of software without the permission of the copyright holder.
A legal agreement that gives the user permission to use software under stated conditions.
End User Licence Agreement: the terms a user accepts, showing what they may and may not do with the software.
Creations of the mind, such as software, music and designs, that are legally owned.
A unique code that must be entered to activate software, used to prevent unauthorised copies.
Technology used by owners to control how digital content is used and to stop illegal copying.
Software modified to remove or bypass its copy protection or licence checks.
A licence allowing an organisation to install software on all its computers, usually for a set fee.
Breaking copyright law by using or copying a protected work without permission.
Limited legal copying for purposes such as research, private study, criticism or review.
A visible or hidden marking in content that shows ownership and can help trace illegal copies.
A person or group affected by a decision or law, such as developers, users and employers.

worked.ans: The Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988 has been broken because the company is using 30 more copies of the software than it has permission (licences) for, so the copyright owner has not been paid.
worked.q: A company buys 10 licences for a graphics program but installs it on 40 computers. Which law has been broken and why? (2 marks)
steps: Identify the action: installing more copies than the licence allows.
Identify the law: this is unauthorised copying/use of protected software.
Explain: the copyright holder has only given permission for 10 installations.

worked.ans: The company can require a unique licence key to be entered during installation (1), so the software will not run unless a valid code is supplied (1). It can use online activation (1), where the program checks with the company's server and limits how many devices can use the same key (1).
worked.q: Describe two ways a software company can reduce illegal copying of its software. (4 marks)
steps: Choose two methods: licence key and online activation (or DRM).
For each, say what it is and how it prevents copying.

worked.ans: For the user, pirated copies may contain malware that damages their files (1) and they will not receive updates or technical support (1). For the developer, each pirated copy is a lost sale (1), so they have less money to fix bugs and produce new products (1).
worked.q: Explain why using pirated software could be a problem for a user and for the software developer. (4 marks)
steps: User impacts: malware risk, no updates or support.
Developer impacts: lost income, less money for development.
